statement: If a rational and a medial area be added together, four irrational straight lines arise, namely a binomial or a first bimedial or a major or a side of a rational plus a medial area.
heath_proof: Let AB be rational, and CD medial; I say that the “side” of the area AD is a binomial or a first bimedial or a major or a side of a rational plus a medial area. For AB is either greater or less than CD. First, let it be greater; let a rational straight line EF be set out, let there be applied to EF the rectangle EG equal to AB, producing EH as breadth, and let HI, equal to DC, be applied to EF, producing HK as breadth. Then, since AB is rational and is equal to EG, therefore EG is also rational. And it has been applied to EF, producing EH as breadth; therefore EH is rational and commensurable in length with EF. [X. 20] Again, since CD is medial and is equal to HI, therefore HI is also medial. And it is applied to the rational straight line EF, producing HK as breadth; therefore HK is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [X. 22] And, since CD is medial, while AB is rational, therefore AB is incommensurable with CD, so that EG is also incommensurable with HI. But, as EG is to HI, so is EH to HK; [VI. 1] therefore EH is also incommensurable in length with HK. [X. 11] And both are rational; therefore EH, HK are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore EK is a binomial straight line, divided at H. [X. 36] And, since AB is greater than CD, while AB is equal to EG and CD to HI, therefore EG is also greater than HI; therefore EH is also greater than HK. The square, then, on EH is greater than the square on HK either by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with EH or by the square on a straight line incommensurable with it. First, let the square on it be greater by the square on a straight line commensurable with itself. Now the greater straight line HE is commensurable in length with the rational straight line EF set out; therefore EK is a first binomial. [X. Deff. II. 1] But EF is rational; and, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and the first binomial, the side of the square equal to the area is binomial. [X. 54] Therefore the “side” of EI is binomial; so that the “side” of AD is also binomial. Next, let the square on EH be greater than the square on HK by the square on a straight line incommensurable with EH. Now the greater straight line EH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line EF set out; therefore EK is a fourth binomial. [X. Deff. II. 4] But EF is rational; and, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and the fourth binomial, the “side” of the area is the irrational straight line called major. [X. 57] Therefore the “side” of the area EI is major; so that the “side” of the area AD is also major. Next, let AB be less than CD; therefore EG is also less than HI, so that EH is also less than HK. Now the square on HK is greater than the square on EH either by the square on a straight line commensurable with HK or by the square on a straight line incommensurable with it. First, let the square on it be greater by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with itself. Now the lesser straight line EH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line EF set out; therefore EK is a second binomial. [X. Deff. II. 2] But EF is rational, and, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and the second binomial, the side of the square equal to it is a first bimedial; [X. 55] therefore the “side” of the area EI is a first bimedial, so that the “side” of AD is also a first bimedial. Next, let the square on HK be greater than the square on HE by the square on a straight line incommensurable with HK. Now the lesser straight line EH is commensurable with the rational straight line EF set out; therefore EK is a fifth binomial. [X. Deff. II. 5] But EF is rational; and, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and the fifth binomial, the side of the square equal to the area is a side of a rational plus a medial area. [X. 58] Therefore the “side” of the area EI is a side of a rational plus a medial area, so that the “side” of the area AD is also a side of a rational plus a medial area.
ai_proof_text:
10.71
**Statement:** If a rational and a medial area be added together, four irrational straight lines arise, namely a binomial or a first bimedial or a major or a side of a rational plus a medial area.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the rational area and CD the medial area. Set out a rational straight line EF and take it as the assigned rational straight line, so that the square on EF is the rational square: areas commensurable with it are rational and areas incommensurable with it are irrational [D10.1.3, D10.1.4]. To EF apply, in a right angle, the rectangle EG equal to AB, producing EH as breadth [1.44, applied successively to the triangles into which AB is divided, in the manner of 1.45]. EG is the rectangle contained by EF, EH, and its side HG opposite to EF is equal to EF [1.34].

**Step 2.** Produce EH to K [P2]. Since the angle EHG is right, the angles EHG, GHK which HG makes with the straight line EK are together equal to two right angles, so the angle GHK is right [1.13]. To HG apply, in the right angle GHK, the rectangle HI equal to CD, producing HK as breadth [1.44, 1.45]; HK lies along EH produced, so EK is one straight line and the rectangle EI contained by EF, EK is made up of EG and HI. Therefore EI is equal to AB together with CD [CN2], and the "side" of EI, namely the straight line the square on which is equal to EI [D10.1.4], is the straight line whose square equals the sum of the rational and the medial area.

**Step 3.** EG is equal to the rational area AB, so EG is rational; and it is applied to the rational straight line EF. Therefore its breadth EH is rational and commensurable in length with EF [10.20].

**Step 4.** CD is a medial area, that is, it is equal to the square on a medial straight line, the side of a rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.21]. Hence HI is equal to the square on a medial straight line, and it is applied to HG; HG is equal to EF and is therefore commensurable with EF and rational [D10.1.1, D10.1.3]. Therefore the breadth HK is rational and incommensurable in length with HG [10.22], and hence incommensurable in length with EF, since HG is equal to EF and a common measure of HK, EF would be a common measure of HK, HG [D10.1.1].

**Step 5.** AB is rational, so AB is commensurable with the square on EF [D10.1.4]. CD is medial, hence irrational [10.21], that is, incommensurable with the square on EF [D10.1.4]. Since AB is commensurable with the square on EF, and the square on EF is incommensurable with CD, AB is incommensurable with CD [10.13]. As EG is equal to AB and HI to CD, any common measure of EG, HI would be a common measure of AB, CD; therefore EG is incommensurable with HI [D10.1.1].

**Step 6.** The rectangles EG, HI stand on the bases EH, HK and have the same height, EF being equal to HG; therefore EG : HI = EH : HK [6.1]. Since EG is incommensurable with HI, EH is incommensurable in length with HK [10.11].

**Step 7.** EH and HK are rational [Steps 3, 4], so each of them is commensurable in square with EF [D10.1.3]; thus the squares on EH and on HK are each commensurable with the square on EF, and therefore are commensurable with one another [10.12], so that EH, HK are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. But they are incommensurable in length [Step 6]. Therefore EH, HK are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and EK, their sum, is a binomial straight line whose terms are EH, HK [10.36].

**Step 8.** Since AB is incommensurable with CD, AB is not equal to CD, for equal magnitudes are measured by one and the same measure [D10.1.1]. Therefore either AB is greater than CD, or AB is less than CD.

**Step 9.** Case I: let AB be greater than CD. Then EG is greater than HI. Since EG : HI = EH : HK [Step 6], and EG exceeds HI, taking each of the four magnitudes once as its own equimultiple shows that EH exceeds HK [D5.5]. Thus EH is the greater term of the binomial EK, and EH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line EF set out [Step 3]. The square on EH exceeds the square on HK by the square on some straight line, and this straight line is either commensurable or incommensurable in length with EH.

**Step 10.** Case I(a): let the square on EH be greater than the square on HK by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with EH. Since the greater term EH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line EF set out, EK is a first binomial [D10.2.1]. The area EI is contained by the rational straight line EF and the first binomial EK; therefore the side of EI is the irrational straight line called binomial [10.54].

**Step 11.** Case I(b): let the square on EH be greater than the square on HK by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with EH. Since the greater term EH is commensurable in length with EF, EK is a fourth binomial [D10.2.4]. The area EI is contained by the rational straight line EF and the fourth binomial EK; therefore the side of EI is the irrational straight line called major [10.57].

**Step 12.** Case II: let AB be less than CD. Then HI is greater than EG, and since EG : HI = EH : HK [Step 6], HK exceeds EH [D5.5]. Thus HK is the greater term and EH the lesser term of the binomial EK, and the lesser term EH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line EF set out [Step 3]. The square on HK exceeds the square on EH by the square on some straight line, either commensurable or incommensurable in length with HK.

**Step 13.** Case II(a): let the square on HK be greater than the square on EH by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with HK. Since the lesser term EH is commensurable in length with EF, EK is a second binomial [D10.2.2]. The area EI is contained by the rational straight line EF and the second binomial EK; therefore the side of EI is the irrational straight line called first bimedial [10.55].

**Step 14.** Case II(b): let the square on HK be greater than the square on EH by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with HK. Since the lesser term EH is commensurable in length with EF, EK is a fifth binomial [D10.2.5]. The area EI is contained by the rational straight line EF and the fifth binomial EK; therefore the side of EI is the irrational straight line called the side of a rational plus a medial area [10.58].

**Step 15.** The cases of Steps 9 and 12, each with its two sub-cases, exhaust all possibilities [Step 8]. Therefore the straight line the square on which is equal to the sum AB + CD of a rational and a medial area is, according to the case, a binomial, a major, a first bimedial, or a side of a rational plus a medial area; so when a rational and a medial area are added together, these four irrational straight lines arise. Q.E.D.

Path note: the proof applies both areas to one rational straight line and classifies the binomial breadth EK by the definitions D10.2; the passage from the order of the binomial to the side of the area uses 10.54, 10.55, 10.57, 10.58 directly. The third and sixth binomials (10.56, 10.59) cannot occur, because the term EH is always commensurable in length with EF.
